wines.name: La Muse Papilles, Côtes du Rhône Rosé

peak.note: As a biodynamically farmed Grenache and Syrah rosé, it is now past its brightest youthful phase, with the fresh red berry and citrus fruit softening into a rounder, more savory style that should be enjoyed soon before the delicate aromatics fade.

wines.name: Beausoleil Rosé, Côtes de Thau IGP

peak.note: As a fresh, unoaked Mediterranean rosé built on Cinsault and Grenache, it is at its most vibrant while young, and the delicate red-berry and citrus fruit will gradually fade into softer, flatter notes as the bright acidity loosens with time.

This Aglianico rosé is a fresh, youthful wine whose bright red berry fruit and zesty acidity are at their most vivid now, and since it is made for early drinking rather than cellaring, it will gradually lose its aromatic lift and crispness with further bottle age.

As a Merlot-based Niagara rosé, it is already past its first flush of bright strawberry and watermelon and is best enjoyed now while the crisp acidity still lifts the fruit, since rosé of this style does not gain complexity with cellaring and will gradually turn soft and dull.

This skin-contact Pinot Grigio is a youthful, fresh-fruited wine right now, showing coppery pear and apricot with gentle tannic grip, and its modest structure means it is best enjoyed in its vibrant early life before the delicate fruit fades.

This sec Chenin from Huet's Haut-Lieu is still tight and youthful, its ripe orchard fruit and chalky, wet-stone minerality held in check by firm acidity that will slowly unfold into honeyed, waxy complexity with bottle age.

A cool, wet and challenging growing season produced a lean, high-acid Sancerre that is showing crisp citrus, green herb and flinty minerality in its fresh youth, and its taut structure will soften only modestly with short cellaring, so it is best enjoyed while the vibrant fruit is at the forefront.

This young Chablis is still tightly wound, with crisp citrus, green apple and flinty minerality that will gradually soften into a rounder, more honeyed texture as the cool, challenging growing season's high acidity integrates with time in bottle.

This regional Chardonnay from a warm, ripe vintage is showing generous orchard fruit and a rounded, fleshy texture now, with its gentle acidity and modest structure meaning it is best enjoyed in its fresh, expressive youth rather than cellared for long.

This Roussanne is still in its youthful, fruit-driven phase with pear, white peach and herbal-floral notes, and its moderate acidity and textural richness suggest it will gain honeyed, nutty complexity gradually rather than rushing toward decline.

This Alto Adige Pinot Grigio is a young, crisp white built for freshness, showing bright orchard fruit, citrus zest and a clean mineral snap from its high-altitude vineyards that will gently soften into more rounded, honeyed notes over the next couple of years.

This Eisacktal Grüner Veltliner from steep granite and slate terraces is still in its fresh, taut youth, with citrus, white pepper and green apple tones framed by bright mineral acidity, and it should gain a subtle honeyed, nutty depth as it settles in bottle.

This Friulian Sauvignon Blanc is in its fresh, vibrant youth, with crisp citrus, passion fruit and herbal notes that are best enjoyed now before the aromatic intensity gradually fades, as the wine is made for early drinking rather than long cellaring.

The oak influence from barrel fermentation is knitting together with the ripe orchard fruit and chalky mineral backbone, so the wine is moving from youthful tension toward a rounder, more savory and honeyed expression while still holding enough freshness to carry it gracefully.

Le Creete, the old-vine Turbiana cru from clay-rich soils south of Lake Garda, is still in its fresh, citrus-driven youth with a saline backbone, and it is just beginning to gain the almond and honeyed depth that Lugana is known for as it ages.

Grisela's volcanic-soil Garganega is showing bright almond, white flower and citrus fruit with a saline, mineral backbone, and its firm acidity and textural depth mean it is still tightening and gaining complexity rather than fading.

Born of a hot, drought-stressed and frost-hit growing season that yielded ripe but low-acid fruit, this Tai is now past its fresh youthful stage and showing softer, rounder honeyed stone fruit with gentle almond and herbal notes, so it is best enjoyed soon while its remaining acidity still gives lift.

This Pigato is showing vivid herbal, citrus and saline coastal freshness with a gentle waxy texture, and its firm acidity and modest alcohol suggest it will hold its brightness for a few more years before the aromatics begin to fade into honeyed, nutty tones.

Tiberio's old-vine Trebbiano Abruzzese from limestone and clay soils is still in its youthful, tightly wound phase, showing citrus, white flowers and crushed stone over a saline backbone, and as the bright acidity and fine phenolic grip slowly integrate it should gain honeyed, almond-tinged complexity.

Still youthful and tightly wound, this Greco shows crisp citrus, white peach and flinty mineral tension that should gradually broaden into honeyed, almond-tinged complexity as the volcanic-soil acidity softens.

This young Vermentino is in its fresh, vibrant phase, showing crisp citrus, green apple and saline minerality from Sardinian coastal sites, and it is best enjoyed soon while its bright aromatics and lively acidity remain at their most expressive.

This is a young, fresh Arneis whose pear, white peach and almond-blossom fruit is at its most vivid now, with crisp acidity and a subtle bitter-almond finish that will gently soften and gain waxy, honeyed nuance but is best enjoyed in its first couple of years.

As a very young Albarín Blanco from Tierra de León, it is currently showing its freshest side with crisp citrus, stone fruit and herbal notes, and its lively acidity and modest structure favor drinking it early rather than aging it long.

Garnacha Blanca from Terra Alta's limestone-rich soils is moving from primary citrus and white-flower freshness into a rounder, waxier phase with honeyed almond and herbal notes, while its saline backbone and moderate acidity keep it balanced and supple rather than flabby.

Coming from a hot, drought-stressed growing season that yielded small, concentrated berries, this Xarel-lo is showing ripe orchard fruit and saline, chalky texture, with its firm natural acidity and light lees character still keeping it fresh while gentle waxy and nutty complexity slowly begins to build.

The wine is still in its bright, primary phase with crisp citrus and green apple fruit held together by firm acidity, and as it ages it should slowly begin to gain the honeyed, petrol-tinged complexity that Niagara Riesling is known for.

This Marlborough Sauvignon Blanc is in its vibrant youth, with zesty citrus, passionfruit and fresh herbal character still front and center thanks to the region's bright acidity, and it should be enjoyed while that aromatic lift remains rather than waiting for slow, subtle development.

Still youthful and tightly wound, the wine shows crisp lime and green apple fruit with a chalky, mineral-driven acid backbone, and as bottle age builds it will begin to unfold toward toasty, honeyed kerosene complexity thanks to Eden Valley's cool elevation and naturally high acidity.
Still tightly wound and dominated by primary dark cherry and plum fruit, with the firm Pommard tannins and structure needing time in bottle to soften and let earthier, savory complexity emerge.

wines.name: Volnay Premier Cru Clos des Angles

peak.note: The ripe, generous 2018 fruit is still youthful and plush, with Volnay's silky tannins and floral perfume beginning to knit together, though the wine will gain more savory, earthy complexity with further bottle age.

This natural, low-sulfur Gamay from Morgon granite and manganese soils is currently showing vibrant crunchy red and dark cherry fruit with a lifted mineral spine, and as the youthful grip softens over the coming seasons it should gain savory, earthy depth while keeping its fresh, juicy character.

The 2020 growing season gave concentrated, ripe fruit with firm but polished tannins, so this wine is still youthful and tight now, with dark cassis and plum framed by structure that will soften and gain cedar and tobacco complexity with further bottle age.

Pauillac's hot, dry 2018 summer gave this Cabernet-led blend ripe, concentrated dark fruit with firm but polished tannins, and it is currently in a youthful, slightly closed phase where cassis and graphite are beginning to knit together with decanting helping considerably.

This Saint-Estèphe is still in its tightly wound youth, with dense dark fruit and firm, slightly rustic tannins that need time to soften, though the vintage's ripeness and freshness point to a steady, rewarding evolution in the cellar.

The 2019 Le Crock is still in its youthful, tightly wound phase, with dense dark fruit and firm Saint-Estèphe tannins that are only beginning to soften, so it rewards decanting now but will reward patience far more.

This fifth-growth Pauillac is still tightly wound and primary, with dense cassis fruit, firm but ripe tannins and fresh acidity from a warm, dry growing season, so it rewards patience or a long decant if opened now.

This Right Bank wine from a warm, concentrated vintage is still youthful, with ripe plum and dark cherry fruit, firm but polished tannins, and a savory Cabernet Franc lift that are only beginning to integrate, so decanting now rewards patience while further cellaring will bring more complexity.

This Cornas is still in its dense, youthful phase, with brooding blackberry, olive and smoky granite notes held in check by firm, mineral tannins that need more time in bottle to soften and integrate.

Still youthful and tightly wound, with dense dark-fruit concentration from a warm, dry growing season now framed by firm tannins and fresh acidity that need time to knit together and let the garrigue, spice and savory complexity emerge.

Still tightly coiled and youthful, this Hermitage shows dense dark fruit, smoked meat and violet beneath firm, grippy tannins that need time to soften, and its concentrated, ripe 2018 fruit and structure promise a long, graceful evolution.

This pure Sangiovese from Panzano's Conca d'Oro is still tightly wound and primary, with dark cherry fruit, firm yet ripe tannins and fresh acidity from a warm, well-balanced growing season, so it will reward patience as the structure softens and savory, earthy, tobacco-tinged complexity emerges.

The 2016 growing season in Oltrepò Pavese gave balanced ripeness with good acidity, and this Pinot Nero is now moving from primary red cherry fruit into savory tertiary notes of forest floor, dried herbs and gentle spice, with fine-grained tannins that have softened but still provide structure.

The tannins that were firm and grippy in youth are now softening, letting the dark cherry and plum fruit of Croatina and Barbera show alongside emerging earthy, spiced and savory notes, while the Uva Rara adds a lifted floral edge, so it is entering a generous, harmonious phase with enough acidity to hold structure for several more years.

This youthful Veneto Pinot Nero is still in its fresh, primary phase, showing bright red cherry and wild strawberry fruit with soft tannins that make it approachable now, though it lacks the structure and concentration for long cellaring.

This youthful Barbera is currently showing bright cherry and plum fruit with its characteristic lively acidity, and as an entry-level bottling made for freshness rather than long cellaring it is best enjoyed in its fruity prime before the vibrancy begins to fade.

Coming from a hot, dry growing season that yielded ripe, generous fruit with softer tannins than classic years, this classic cooperative Barbaresco is still tight and primary, showing cherry and rose with firm structure that needs time in bottle to unwind and gain tertiary complexity.

Borgogno's entry-level Langhe Nebbiolo from a warm, concentrated vintage is still youthful and primary, with ripe red cherry fruit and firm but polished tannins that will soften and bring out rose and tar nuances with a little cellar time.

Still youthful and tightly coiled, this classically structured Barolo shows firm tannins and bright acidity wrapped around cherry, rose petal and tar notes that need time in bottle to knit together, so decanting well ahead is advised if opened now.

Still tightly wound and youthful, its firm tannins and bright acidity are slowly integrating with the sour cherry, rose and tar fruit, so it rewards patience or a long decant before the savory, earthy complexity emerges.

Still tightly wound and youthful, the Monvigliero's perfumed rose petal and wild cherry fruit sits behind firm, fine-grained tannins that need time to soften, though its limestone-driven freshness and the vintage's balanced ripeness point to graceful, long-lived evolution.

This Rùfina Sangiovese is still in its youthful phase, with bright cherry fruit and the region's characteristic fresh acidity and firm tannins beginning to soften, though the cooler, wetter 2023 growing season leaves it more lively and savory than opulent, so it rewards short-term cellaring over long aging.

Fontodi's Chianti Classico from a warm, dry vintage is showing ripe dark cherry and plum fruit with supple tannins and the estate's signature Panzano freshness, still youthful and tightly knit, so it will gain savory, earthy complexity with a little more bottle time.

This young Sangiovese from a fresh, balanced Montalcino season is still showing primary cherry and red-berry fruit with lively acidity and firm but fine tannins, and it will soften into more savory, earthy complexity as it settles in bottle.

The 2018 Cordella is still youthful and tightly wound, with sour cherry, dried herbs and fine-grained tannins that are gradually softening, so decanting now rewards patience while the more savory, earthy complexity of Sangiovese slowly emerges.

wines.name: Brunello di Montalcino Riserva Madonna del Piano

peak.note: Still tightly wound and in its youth, this structured, long-lived Sangiovese from a classic cool, balanced Montalcino vintage is slowly shedding its firm tannins to reveal layers of dark cherry, iris, tobacco and sweet spice, and it will reward further patience or a long decant if opened now.

The wine is still in its fruit-driven youth, with bright cherry and blackcurrant supported by firm but ripening tannins from the Cabernet that should soften and integrate with the Sangiovese's acidity over the coming years.

This youthful Rosso Piceno is showing bright cherry and plum fruit with soft tannins from its Montepulciano backbone, and a cooler, rain-affected season left it fresh and approachable rather than dense, so it is best enjoyed for its vibrant fruit over long cellaring.

The wine is still in its fruit-driven youth, with dark cherry and plum framed by firm but ripening tannins and oak spice that are gradually integrating, so it rewards decanting now while the structure from Abruzzo's warm, well-ripened vintage slowly unwinds toward more savory, leathery complexity.

This Cannonau is still in its vibrant youth, with ripe red cherry and wild herb fruit carried by soft tannins and sun-warmed Sardinian generosity, so it drinks best now while the fruit stays fresh before slowly moving toward dried fruit and earthy spice.

The warm, ripe 2022 season gave this old-vine Mencía from steep slate terraces generous red and black fruit softened by fine tannins, yet the wine still shows enough mineral tension and fresh acidity to keep gaining savory, earthy complexity in the bottle.

The warm, ripe 2022 vintage gave this Mencía generous dark cherry fruit with softer tannins than usual, yet the slate-driven acidity and subtle stem-inclusive structure keep it fresh, so it is open and charming now while still tightening into more savory, mineral complexity as it settles.

The wine is still in its fresh, youthful phase, with bright red fruit, volcanic mineral tension and light peppery spice that are just beginning to knit together, and its high-altitude acidity and low-extraction structure should carry it gracefully toward more savory, earthy complexity.

The 2021 Orchard Block from Dundee Hills volcanic Jory soils is moving out of its tight, youthful phase, with bright red cherry and cranberry fruit beginning to layer in forest floor, dried rose and gentle spice as the fine-grained tannins and fresh acidity from a warm but balanced growing season integrate.

wines.name: Cabernet Sauvignon
wines.region: Happy Canyon of Santa Barbara, California

peak.note: Happy Canyon's warm days and cool nights gave this Cabernet ripe dark fruit, firm structure and a bright acid spine, so it is still tightening its tannins and slowly layering cassis and cedar with early hints of tobacco and earth, rewarding a decant now but better with a few more years of cellaring.

This warm, even vintage gave ripe, generous fruit and polished tannins, and the wine is now moving from primary blackcurrant and plum toward cedar, graphite and dried herb nuances while its structure remains supple and well integrated.

The warm, well-ripened 2019 Niagara growing season gave this Bordeaux-style blend supple tannins and dark fruit that are now softening into savory cedar, tobacco and dried herb notes, so it is drinking nicely with decanting while still holding enough structure to evolve gracefully.

The 2020 growing season in Niagara delivered ripe, balanced fruit, and this structured Cabernet Franc is now softening its tannins while its red berry, graphite and dried herb character begins to gain savory, tobacco-leaf complexity.

The warm, steady growing season gave this Syrah ripe dark fruit and supple tannins that are now softening, while peppery spice and savory, smoky notes begin to emerge alongside the cool-climate freshness that keeps it lively and balanced.

As a very young Mendoza Malbec from an entry-level Alto Molino bottling, it is currently showing exuberant plum and blackberry fruit with firm, youthful tannins that should soften gracefully with a little bottle age.

As the second wine of Nairac from a vintage marked by a warm, patchy botrytis season, it is showing honeyed apricot, orange marmalade and saffron with a fresh acidic backbone, offering charm and approachability now while still holding the structure to evolve gracefully toward deeper nutty, caramelised notes.

w-serenissima-prosecco-millesimato.hook: Made from the Glera grape in Italy's Veneto, it's the only sparkling wine we pour by the glass.
w-serenissima-prosecco-millesimato.pitch: It's light and fresh, with lively bubbles and soft pear and apple fruit, so it's an easy, cheerful way to start a meal. At $16 a glass, you can have bubbles without committing to a whole bottle.
w-serenissima-prosecco-millesimato.taste: Light, frothy and fresh, usually with pear, green apple and a soft, gently fruity finish.
w-serenissima-prosecco-millesimato.grape: Glera, the grape on the label, gives this wine its light body and fresh, fruity, easy-drinking character.
w-serenissima-prosecco-millesimato.place: It comes from the Veneto in northeast Italy, where Lake Garda and the Adriatic Sea soften the weather, which helps keep the fruit fresh.

dishes.why: The fresh bubbles cut through the creamy burrata, and the fruit sits nicely with the tomato.
It's light enough not to cover up the delicate raw tuna, and its freshness matches the dish's sharp, salty bite.
Light, cool bubbles calm the spice and refresh your mouth between bites of shrimp.

alts.when: Italian bubbles with more depth and richness, by the bottle ($126)
a Champagne by the bottle for a celebration ($125)
a light, fresh white by the glass without bubbles ($15)

qs.q: Which description best fits the Serenissima Prosecco Millesimato?
opts: Light, frothy and fresh, with soft pear and apple fruit
Rich and toasty, with bready notes and fine, firm bubbles
Very sweet and grapey, low in alcohol, like a dessert
Bone-dry and steely, with sharp lemon and chalky notes
qs.why: It's a light, fresh, fruity sparkling wine, not a rich, toasty, very sweet or steely one.

qs.q: Which Italian region is the Serenissima Prosecco Millesimato from?
opts: Veneto
Piedmont
Tuscany
Lombardy
qs.why: It comes from the Veneto in northeast Italy, where the weather is softened by Lake Garda and the Adriatic Sea.

qs.q: What grape is the Serenissima Prosecco Millesimato made from?
qs.why: Glera is the grape named on the label.

qs.q: What size and price is a glass of the Serenissima Prosecco Millesimato?
qs.why: Our other wines by the glass come in 5oz and 8oz, but the Prosecco is poured as a 5oz glass only.

qs.q: A guest starting with the Burrata & Tomato wants a single glass of something sparkling and light. What would you suggest, and why?
key: Serenissima Prosecco Millesimato
It's the only sparkling wine we pour by the glass, at $16 for 5oz
Its light, fresh fruit and bubbles cut through the creamy burrata and suit the tomato

decoys.why: It's sold by the bottle only, so it can't be poured as a single glass.
It's a Champagne sold by the bottle only, not by the glass.
It's bottle only at $215, far more than a guest wanting one glass expects.

wrong: Its heavy, full body stands up to the richness of the cheese.
Its firm tannin grips the creamy burrata and cleans it away.
Its soft, low acidity lets the sweet tomato take over.
qs.why: The guest asked for one glass of light bubbles, and the Prosecco is the only sparkling wine on the list poured by the glass.

qs.q: What grapes go into the Serenissima Prosecco Millesimato, compared with the Ca' del Bosco Franciacorta Cuvée Prestige Brut?
qs.ans: The Prosecco is Glera; the Franciacorta is Chardonnay, Pinot Nero and Pinot Bianco
acc: Glera versus Chardonnay, Pinot Nero and Pinot Bianco
Prosecco is Glera, Franciacorta is mostly Chardonnay with Pinot Nero and Pinot Bianco
qs.why: Both are Italian sparkling wines, but they're made from different grapes, and that's a big part of why the Prosecco tastes lighter and fruitier.

w-ca-del-bosco-franciacorta-cuvee-presti.hook: Ca' del Bosco is a classic Franciacorta house, made like Champagne and aged at least 18 months.
w-ca-del-bosco-franciacorta-cuvee-presti.pitch: It's dry and crisp, with fine bubbles and a creamy, lightly toasty depth that feels a step up from Prosecco. If you love Champagne, this is Italy's answer, and it's wonderful with seafood.
w-ca-del-bosco-franciacorta-cuvee-presti.say: KAH del BOSS-koh, fran-chah-KOR-tah, koo-VAY press-TEEZH BROOT
w-ca-del-bosco-franciacorta-cuvee-presti.taste: Dry and crisp, with fine bubbles, lemon and apple fruit, and a creamy, lightly toasty finish.
w-ca-del-bosco-franciacorta-cuvee-presti.grape: It's a blend of Chardonnay, Pinot Nero (Pinot Noir) and Pinot Bianco, and the Chardonnay is a grape that soaks up the creamy, toasty character that comes from long ageing.
w-ca-del-bosco-franciacorta-cuvee-presti.place: Franciacorta in Lombardy, northern Italy, has a mild climate softened by Lake Iseo, and its rules say it can only make sparkling wine in the traditional method, where the second fermentation that makes the bubbles happens in the bottle, just like Champagne.
w-ca-del-bosco-franciacorta-cuvee-presti.producer: Ca' del Bosco is one of the classic producers of Franciacorta, alongside Bellavista and Berlucchi.

serve.glass: white wine glass or tulip-shaped flute

dishes.why: Its crisp freshness and bubbles cut through the rich, salty scallop, and its creamy side matches the sweet sear.
It's dry and fresh enough for delicate fish, with enough depth to stand up to the crisp seared skin and herbs.
The toasty, creamy notes from ageing suit the earthy mushroom, and the bubbles clean up the richness.

alts.when: a Champagne of a similar style ($140)
lighter and fruitier, or by the glass ($16)
a famous Champagne house for a big celebration ($215)

qs.q: Which description best fits the Ca' del Bosco Franciacorta Cuvée Prestige Brut?
opts: Dry and crisp, with fine bubbles and creamy, toasty depth
Soft and frothy, light, with simple pear fruit and sweetness
Sweet and grapey, low in alcohol, best with fruit desserts
Lean and bone-dry, with only sharp green apple and no depth
qs.why: Brut means dry, and at least 18 months resting on its lees (the spent yeast) gives it a creamy, toasty depth.

qs.q: What is the shortest time a non-vintage Franciacorta like the Ca' del Bosco Cuvée Prestige Brut must age on its lees?
opts: 18 months
9 months
36 months
60 months
qs.why: Franciacorta rules say non-vintage wines need at least 18 months on the lees (the spent yeast), which adds texture.

qs.q: Which three grapes go into the Ca' del Bosco Franciacorta Cuvée Prestige Brut?
qs.ans: Chardonnay, Pinot Nero and Pinot Bianco
acc: Chardonnay, Pinot Noir and Pinot Blanc
qs.why: It's a blend of these three grapes, with Chardonnay giving much of its creamy character.

qs.q: Which lake softens the climate where the Ca' del Bosco Franciacorta Cuvée Prestige Brut is grown?
qs.why: Franciacorta's mild climate comes from Lake Iseo and the low hills south of it.

qs.q: A guest ordering the Seared Scallop wants a bottle of dry Italian sparkling wine with some richness, under $130. What would you suggest, and why?
key: Ca' del Bosco Franciacorta Cuvée Prestige Brut
It's dry, Italian and $126, made like Champagne with at least 18 months on its lees for a creamy, toasty richness
Its crisp freshness and fine bubbles cut through the scallop's richness and salt

decoys.why: It's Italian and well under budget, but it's light and simple rather than rich, so it doesn't match what the guest asked for.
It fits the budget at $125, but it's a French Champagne, not Italian.
It's French and $215, well over the guest's budget.

wrong: Its light, thin body keeps out of the way of the scallop.
Its firm tannin grips the seared crust of the scallop.
Its bold red-berry flavour stands up to the sear.
qs.why: It's the only dry Italian sparkling wine on the list with real richness under $130, and its crisp freshness and bubbles suit the rich, salty scallop.

qs.q: Where is the Ca' del Bosco Franciacorta Cuvée Prestige Brut from, compared with the André Chemin Brut Premier Cru?
qs.ans: Ca' del Bosco is from Franciacorta in Lombardy, Italy; André Chemin is a French Champagne
qs.why: Both are dry sparkling wines sold by the bottle at similar prices ($126 and $140), so where they come from is the clearest way to tell them apart for a guest.

w-tarlant-brut-reserve.hook: Real Champagne from Chardonnay, Pinot Noir and Pinot Meunier, aged at least 15 months on its yeast.
w-tarlant-brut-reserve.pitch: This is a true Champagne: dry, crisp and lively, with fine bubbles and a soft, creamy feel from long ageing on its yeast. It wakes up your palate and makes salty, rich starters taste even better, and at $125 it's our friendliest Champagne by the bottle.
w-tarlant-brut-reserve.taste: Dry and crisp, with fresh citrus, fine bubbles and a smooth, creamy texture from resting on its yeast.
w-tarlant-brut-reserve.grape: A blend of Chardonnay, Pinot Noir and Pinot Meunier; Chardonnay is a fairly neutral grape that takes on the winemaker's choices, so here it brings a clean, fresh backbone.
w-tarlant-brut-reserve.place: Champagne in France has a cool climate where grapes barely ripen, which keeps the acidity (the mouth-watering freshness) high, and that is exactly what good sparkling wine needs.

dishes.why: The crisp freshness and bubbles cut through the scallop's richness and love its saltiness.
A light, dry sparkling wine stays delicate next to raw tuna and matches its bright, zesty dressing.
Clean, crisp Champagne suits delicate white fish and lifts the salt and herbs.

alts.when: another Champagne, usually built on Pinot Noir and Chardonnay, at $140
a famous classic Champagne house for a special occasion, $215
by the glass, or a lighter, cheaper sparkling at $16 a glass

qs.q: Which description best fits the Tarlant Brut Réserve NV?
opts: Dry and crisp, with fine bubbles
Sweet and grapey, with soft bubbles
Off-dry and peachy, with frothy bubbles
Rich and honeyed, with gentle bubbles
qs.why: It is a Brut Champagne, so it is dry, with high acidity and fine bubbles.

qs.q: On the Tarlant Brut Réserve NV label, what does the word 'Brut' tell the guest?
opts: The wine is dry
The wine is sweet
The wine is pink
The wine is aged
qs.why: Brut is the French label term for a dry sparkling wine.

qs.q: Which three grapes go into the Tarlant Brut Réserve NV?
qs.ans: Chardonnay, Pinot Noir and Pinot Meunier
acc: Pinot Noir, Pinot Meunier and Chardonnay
the three Champagne grapes: Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, Pinot Meunier
qs.why: The Tarlant uses all three grapes, which a server can mention to sound knowledgeable.

qs.q: By law, at least how long must a non-vintage Champagne like the Tarlant Brut Réserve NV rest on its lees (the spent yeast)?
qs.why: The law says 12 months, though the usual minimum in practice is 15 months, and that time on the yeast adds a creamy texture.

qs.q: A guest has ordered the Seared Scallop and asks for a bottle of real Champagne from France, spending under $130. What would you suggest, and why?

it is genuine Champagne at $125, inside the guest's budget
its crisp acidity and fine bubbles cut through the scallop's richness and suit its saltiness

decoys.why: It is a lovely Champagne, but at $140 it is over the guest's budget.
At $215 it is far over the guest's budget.
It is priced close, at $126, but it is Italian Franciacorta, not Champagne.

wrong: Its heavy, full body stands up to the buttery richness of the scallop
Its firm tannin grips the scallop and balances out its natural sweetness
Its soft, low acidity keeps the delicate scallop feeling gentle and calm
qs.why: The Tarlant is the only Champagne on the list under $130, and its light body and high acidity are what make it work with the scallop.

qs.q: Which grape is in the Tarlant Brut Réserve NV that is not one of the usual grapes in the André Chemin Brut Premier Cru NV?
acc: Pinot Meunier is in the Tarlant
qs.why: The Tarlant uses all three Champagne grapes, while the André Chemin is usually just Pinot Noir and Chardonnay.

w-andre-chemin-brut-premier-cru.hook: Champagne usually built on Pinot Noir and Chardonnay, kept bright and crisp by a cool climate.
w-andre-chemin-brut-premier-cru.pitch: This is a dry, crisp Champagne with fine bubbles and a little more depth from Pinot Noir, a red grape that's usually in the blend. It's elegant enough for a celebration and just as good with mushrooms, fish or roast chicken.
